Explanation: Calling insulin a tool for "weight management" is medically inaccurate and highly misleading. In endocrinology, insulin is known as a primary anabolic (storage) hormone. When there is excess glucose that isn't needed for immediate energy, insulin drives the body to store it as fat (lipogenesis) and actively stops the body from burning stored fat (lipolysis). High insulin levels, insulin resistance, or taking insulin therapy almost universally lead to weight gain, not weight management or weight loss.

Reference: Mayo Clinic - Insulin and weight gain: Keep the pounds off

Explanation: Vaguely defining the Rajya Sabha's special powers as "considering matters of national importance" is factually incorrect. Deliberation on national issues and policy determination are functions shared by both Houses (and largely driven by the Executive accountable to the Lok Sabha). The actual exclusive constitutional powers granted solely to the Rajya Sabha are:

Article 249: Passing a resolution to authorize Parliament to legislate on a state subject in the national interest.

Article 312: Passing a resolution to authorize the creation of one or more new All-India Services.

Article 67: Initiating a resolution for the removal of the Vice-President of India.

Reference: Constitution of India - Articles 249, 312 & 67

Explanation: The Constitution of India does not specify a fixed 5-year term for the Chief Minister. Under Article 164(1), the Chief Minister holds office "during the pleasure of the Governor." In practice, this means the Chief Minister remains in office for as long as they retain the majority support of the State Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha). The 5-year term explicitly defined in Article 172 belongs to the duration of the Legislative Assembly itself, not automatically to the individual holding the office of the Chief Minister.

Reference: Constitution of India - Article 164 & Article 172

Explanation: Under IFAB (International Football Association Board) Law 11, this statement misses several critical technical conditions:

Timing of Judgment: Offside position is strictly evaluated at the exact moment the ball is played or touched by a teammate, not when the receiving player actually gets or touches the ball.

Position vs. Offence: Merely being in an offside position (ahead of the second-last opponent, which usually includes the goalkeeper) is not an offence in itself. A player is only penalized if they become actively involved in play by interfering with play, interfering with an opponent, or gaining an advantage from that position.

Relation to the Ball: A player is never offside if they are level with or behind the ball at the moment it is passed, or if they are in their own half of the field.

Exceptions: An attacker can never be called offside if they receive the ball directly from a throw-in, goal kick, or corner kick.

Reference: IFAB - Laws of the Game (Law 11: Offside)
